options.text: The probability of every possible outcome
A pair of classical bits
One of the qubit's two computational basis states
The physical position of an electron

questions.explanation: A ket labels a quantum state. The computational basis contains |0> and |1>; the notation does not specify a particle's position.

questions.prompt: What is returned by one Z-basis measurement of a qubit?

options.text: One classical outcome, 0 or 1
Both complex amplitudes
A complete Bloch vector
The relative phase as a decimal

questions.explanation: The amplitudes determine the outcome probabilities, but a shot records only one bit. Recovering information about an unknown preparation requires repeated experiments.

questions.prompt: What does a point on the surface of the Bloch sphere describe?

options.text: A physical orbit around an atom
Every possible joint two-qubit state
A histogram of earlier shots
A pure single-qubit state, ignoring global phase

questions.explanation: The sphere represents single-qubit states. Its surface describes pure states, while strictly mixed states are inside.

questions.prompt: The amplitude of |1> is i/2. What is P(1)?
questions.explanation: Use squared magnitude, not the ordinary square of a complex number. The magnitude of i/2 is 1/2, so its probability is 1/4.

options.text: [1/sqrt(2), i/sqrt(2)]

questions.explanation: The two squared magnitudes are 1/2 and 1/2. The other vectors have total squared magnitudes of 2, 1/2 and 4.

questions.prompt: A qubit has amplitudes 3/5 and 4/5. What is P(0)?
questions.explanation: The first entry belongs to |0>. Squaring 3/5 gives 9/25; the remaining probability is 16/25.

questions.prompt: An equal-weight state has amplitudes 1/2 and 1/2 before normalization. Which positive factor normalizes it?

options.text: sqrt(2)
1/sqrt(2)

questions.explanation: Its total squared magnitude is 1/2. Multiplication by sqrt(2) doubles that total, giving unit normalization.

questions.prompt: For the chapter's Bloch formula, theta=pi and phi=0 give which Z outcome?

options.text: 0 with certainty
0 and 1 with equal probabilities
1 with certainty
An outcome determined by phi rather than theta

questions.explanation: The amplitudes are cos(pi/2)=0 and sin(pi/2)=1. This is the south pole, corresponding to |1>.

questions.prompt: Two pure states have the same Bloch latitude but different longitudes. What can their direct Z histograms establish?

options.text: They must be the same state
Their Z probabilities must differ
One of the states is necessarily mixed
They have the same Z probabilities, but may have different relative phases

questions.explanation: Latitude fixes theta and therefore the squared magnitudes. Longitude changes phi, which direct Z measurement does not determine.

questions.prompt: A preparation with P(0)=3/4 is measured four times on fresh copies. Must exactly three outcomes be 0?

options.text: No; three is the expected count, not a guaranteed count
Yes; normalization fixes the count in every group of four
No; every group must instead contain two zeros
Yes; the imaginary amplitude removes randomness

questions.explanation: Probability predicts a distribution over many experiments. A particular four-shot sample can contain anywhere from zero to four zeros.
